blocks.x: Okay, it's going if you want to give your name and how you were born and playing.

You ready? Yes, it's all right. Well, my name is Willie H. Hightower. I was born in Nashville, Tennessee on President Polk's Hill in 1889, October the 23rd, 7.30 in the morning. My mother and father left Nashville, Tennessee when I was six years old and went to New Orleans, Louisiana, which my uncle was living there, my mother's brother. And from time to time, where I grew and I worked for the New Orleans Ice Cream Company, my oldest place that I stayed as long as I did. From the date that I started to work was somewhere around 1908. And I left there in 1915 as I started to play music. And after I started to play music, then I went to my boss one day and told him, Mr. Brown, and told him that I thought that I was going to play music. And he got mad and sold with me and told me that I couldn't quit him. I'd been there too long.
That was the Brown Ice Cream Company.
Yeah, Brown Ice Cream Company. The Orleans Ice Cream Company. I drove a wagon after they got up. And after 1915, I quit.
Oh, if the light is too bright in your eyes, you can turn it off.
No, no, it's not too bright. And after 1915, I decided that I wanted to play music.
Well, can you tell about when you were a boy and worked on Magazine Street there? Yeah.
Yeah.
And Joe Oliver.

Yeah, well, we come along and me and Joe Oliver came along and he worked across the street from me. I went to Tommel of France No. 6 School. Tommel of France No. 6. I forget the name of the school that Joe went to. But every evening we would play with one another with the hoes. His madam would holler at him and my madam would holler at me. But we had to just pump the street, pose across the street at one another. And we were both in short pants at that time. I was going on 10 years old, around 10. And after we grew up, we stayed in the Orleans. And he started to play music for us. Well, when I got in the music business...
What was your first instrument? Did you start on the cornet?

Well, no, I didn't. I started on the cornet, but I put it down. I started to play bass. That was a one-string bass. I had one bass made out of a soapbox. We had an original guitar and an original mandolin. Rob Smith was the guitar player's name. And the mandolin player, I forget his name, but I made me a bass out of one string, out of a cat gut, one string. It went so good until I changed from the soapbox and got a bass with one string on it. And we played that for a while. Well, that didn't last long because in those days, back in the early days, it was the greatest thing in the world for a musician to go around his friend's house and serenade them at night and get something to drink or something to eat. And so we'd wait until everybody got sleep at night. And then we'd sneak up under their window and we had a wasp. The wasp was Merry Widow, wasn't it? And we'd play that. And when they'd all see us and they'd let us in and they'd get up and put on their clothes and they'd give us something to eat and give us something to drink, and we'd go on to somebody else's house until maybe some policeman. Like around my neighborhood, we had an Irish officer by the name of Pat Kennedy, and he'd just get mad with us, and naturally he would run us in, tell us to go on off the street with that person, and we'd run from him, go on, in and out. But that's how I started.
What part of town did you...

That was 6th and Rampart, Rounds, that's where I stayed after most of my time, and after that I grew up, and after I got up in age, I was 17 years old, and I went in business. I opened in New Orleans Ice Cream Paula at 6th and Rampart across from Bazee's Saloon, see. And I was on Rampart Street, two-story building, and Bazeele was right on the corner. Well, after I stayed there a little while, I made such a good business there, until Roy Palmer got in connection with me. And I told him, I said, well, I don't know about playing music, but I had a piano in the place, and I had met Miney Jones, and Miney Jones used to come that night and play, and I used to give him $1.75, something like that, to play, see. Well, after that got to going so good, then I bought the saloon from Smith's at Fulton Rampart. He went to Los Angeles and sold the saloon to me. I even had a saloon and couldn't go in it. I was too young. Police wouldn't let me. I had five servants in that place at 17 years old and run the New Orleans...
New Orleans...

That's right. Ice cream company. New Orleans Ice Cream Paula, we called it. Then at that time, I got so popular, I got me a horse and buggy. Well, in those days, that was around about 1910, I was popular. I got a horse and buggy, and had my horse tied out in front of the place, and bought a saloon, even couldn't go in the saloon, and at that time, had a Chinese cook. Well, that went on all right. Then I sold the saloon. I was asked to sell this saloon. Well, I sold it to a fellow. I don't know whether I got any money out of it or not. And then I had a fellow by the name of Bab Frank that played a piccolo in the office. He was selling crabs up and down the street at night with a white coat on and a basket. And he asked me, he said, you're a businessman. He said, I want to talk to you. He said, how would you like to open up a business with me? And I said, what sort of a business? He says, a long ground. Oh, I said, that would be all right. And he was playing with a salsa band from downtown. He played piccolo. And selling crabs in the daytime, see. And so I opened up a business. We opened up a long ground at Sixth and Rampart. It was called the Sixth and Rampart Long Ground. Right back of Plummer's Horseshoe Shop. Had a horseshoe, horseshoe horses in the front. And the back of his place was a long ground. I went to work and put in a platform there. Built a band stand. And my first band that I hired in there was Freddie Kepler.
Oh, yeah.

He got Freddie Kepler. Is that the Olympia or what was the name? That was, I think that was the Olympia. Bab Frank was leading the band. But Freddie Kepler was the main man. And they supposed to have a guitar player in the band. It was the greatest that we ever was in the Orleans. And I forget his name now. He was a dog, brown skin. All them boys lived down in Frenchwater town, see.
And it was Bud Scott, was it?
No, it wasn't Bud Scott, no. Bud Scott, no. Bud Scott wasn't John. He was this older man than Bud Scott.
Older man.
Yeah, he was an old fellow. Very sensible fellow. Great man. Can't think of his name. Wasn't Brock? No. What?
Brock Mumford. Brock Mumford. He played with Bolton and Frankie Dewson. I don't know those guitar players.

No, I don't know this guitar player either because he was a very sensible fellow. He didn't drink and he didn't smoke, you see. And he tried to carry the band on straight. Well, I kept that place going for two summers. And after then I started playing music. Roy Palmer brought me a horn. And the first thing that I did, Roy brought the horn by there about eight o'clock that night. And it was brass. And the greatest thing that I wanted to see, that horn shine. So I just waited until the next day and brought me some brass polish for my horses that I used, my mules on the polish. And I polish that come home and polish that horn up. And run some water through it. And fool around with it a little while. After a while I committed to getting sensible to it.
Did you have any lessons when you started? No.

Had your father or mother anyone played any? My father was a musician and my mother was a musician. She played harp. My father played E flat cornet in a brass band. He was a barber. He was everything. He was a barber and he was a sport man. He'd run dog fights and cock fights in Tennessee, in Nashville, see. And he had a barber shop on Churchin Hill in Tennessee with 11 Negro barbers in his cell, white, I mean his cell, made it 12th. The barbers? Yeah. Nothing but white trade. He stayed there. I forget how many years. Now it was. But at the same time, we'll get back.
One more question. Where did your mother play harp? Did she play?
No, she didn't bring her harp away from, no. She didn't, of course it was.
Can you remember the earliest music you ever heard? Was it them, your parents playing?
Did I hear?
Oh, yes. That's the first music. Did you hear any music in the churches when you were young?
Well, at that age, I didn't go to church that much.
Which church did you go to?

I don't remember that. I can't remember that. Were you Catholic or Protestant? We were Protestants. Protestants. What do you call it? It's Protestant, same as Methodist. Yes, Methodist is what I wanted to do. Yes, that's right. And I didn't hear my father play, but I had pictures up until the time I left New Orleans and I lost most of that stuff, see. Thought I was going back to New Orleans and never got back. But my mother played a harp. She didn't bring her harp to New Orleans. After she got a New Orleans, she got a piano. And she played the piano a while. And after things, my grandmother died, then she got a guitar and she played the guitar. Well, all three of the instruments are practically the same, see. But my father was an E-flat trumpet player in a brass band, see. And I had his uniforms. I think I got a picture now somewhere with him, with his uniform, see.
Can you tell the first job you played then in music?
In the music, yes.
Was that with Roy?

Roy brought me a horn. I shined the horn up, cleaned the horn. About an hour after I cleaned the horn and was sitting down in the back. There wasn't much during that night and my knee wasn't there. I didn't use him until late at night anyway. Roy come in. And I said, yeah, man, I'm pulling with this thing. I'm going to play it. And he showed me then how to blow and how to play on the instrument, see. But it seemed like I had so much ambition I didn't want even Roy to show me I liked the trumpet because my father played a trumpet. But this instrument that I played wasn't a trumpet. It was a C-G-York-Connet. And six and a half or seven inch bell on it, big as a trombone now. Big bell with a little shirt. Yeah, big bell on it. See, that's what I had. And I just thought it was the greatest thing in the world. And Roy talked to me a while. He sat down, he had some ice cream, he went on out about his business. I fooled around. Kept on fooling with it every evening as I come in. About, I guess it was about three weeks after I had this horn, Roy come by there and said, we're going to form a band together. He said, I'm going to teach you how to play. And if I don't teach you how to play, he says, with your backing, he says, we can get somewhere. See? See? You've got the business. And he said, use the idea of your business for the music business. So that went on. That quarters. Yeah. So that went on that way. Now I stayed. I can't think of the number of the place, but it was on Rampart near Washington. See, that's Fifth Street. It's Fourth, then it's Washington, then it's Sixth Street going uptown, see? And this man had been passing there every night. He looked like a white man. But I never paid much attention to him. And naturally, I guess he heard me back in that plane at night. And this man was Dave Poikins, the first trombone player in the French Opera House, if I'm all right? No, Tulane Theater.
He played with the white musicians too, right?
He didn't play with nothing else but the white. But he was living Sixth and Verone.
Oh, really? I've been there, yeah.

See, he was living Sixth and Verone. So one night, he heard me and he come on in. And the person that I had in the store asked him, did he want anything? He said, no, I want to see the person that's blowing that horn. And he's a very swell fellow, see? Very swell. And he spoke to me and told me who he was. He says, are you taking music lessons? I said, no, sir. I don't want no music lessons. I said, all I want to do is play like Freddie Kepler and Joe Oliver.
See?

And he laughed. He says, no. He says, Joe Oliver is all right. Freddie Kepler's all right. He said, but you want to learn music. Oh, I said, I'll learn all right. He said, but you better watch yourself. And he couldn't talk and he went on down the street. Well, every evening he'd pass by there going home, not late at night, but it'd be in the early part of the night. I'd see him maybe three or four times a week. So Roy knew music. But Roy never coaxed me with the music end of it. Roy, to teach me how to play, he'd bring his trombone down there. And he'd tell me to follow him. Now the music, he figured I could pick up when I got ready. But I liked music. I liked the idea of music. So after about a week's practice me and Roy had, Freddie Kepler gave Roy a job back Tulane Avenue somewhere, somewhere around Tulane, Laperone, somewhere back in there, see? And it was a concert and a dance afterwards. And at them times, as I learned in later years, that dance bands hadn't been out very long. You see, that was around 1909, 1910. Well, they hadn't been out very long. And Roy got the band together. We got a fellow by the name of Pep Wallace on bass, Roy Palmer on trombone, myself on conant, and didn't even have a case for it. I wrapped it up in newspaper and kept it on the job that night. And I couldn't blow it. It didn't take no chance of blowing it because I guess I had more of a idea of clowning. And it was something that the people had never seen. And I always did believe in playing, like you see Lionel Hampton, them doing, say something when they do. It's like Dots used to do. Dots would sit by the drums and say, like that all night long, see? Couldn't tell what he was doing. Well, that was mine. Was that the drummer? Baby Dots, yeah. Oh, Baby Dots. Yeah. I got Baby Dots on drums, Pep Wallace on bass, Rob Smith on guitar, Roy Palmer on trombone, myself on conant, didn't use no piano. Seven pieces. And Sidney Bechet on climbing. Well, we got him a pair of long pants, see, because we decided all old musicians that was in long pants went in and played. We'd get long pants for the youngsters. So many of the youngsters. I had to get long pants for Baby Dots. I had to carry his drums, see, because he was very small. And whenever we went anywhere on a job, I had to carry his drum because his drum was about that high. You know how high the brass band drums would be? Would they rope someone and spit on them and pull them? Well, that was his first drum. And to eliminate the load, we didn't use no snare drum. We used a banjo head, broke the head off of a banjo and tied it in a chair. And Baby Dots played on that. That's what he played on. And the pedal was a flow pedal. The Ludwig, the leadies wasn't out. The leadies, I think, was the overhead pedal, the last pedal was out. Was the pedals up? Did you see the Ludwig pedals on the flow? Well, the Ludwig pedals only come up just to the beater. The cymbal attached onto the bass drum. You don't see nothing like that now. We had a cymbal attached onto the bass drum. I didn't see that, I remember that. Well, that's what we had, and that's what I hated to carry, was that cymbal. And that flow pedal, I think it was a Ludwig. You see, Ludwig come ahead of Ludwig in later years when they come up with that overhead pedal. Down here it just had a piece of wood, and it come from a spring from the top, and the cymbal set on the top of your drum. You understand? I'm saying pictures of him. Yeah. And we went out to that night and played that concert. They had a girl playing the accent. Then it got so good until all the boys in the band and Roy, we went and set in with this girl, was playing this concert. And the people just admired the band. After then, there was nothing I could do. I couldn't play, so I just held the horn in my hand and walked on the music stand in front of the band, and clapped my hands. The rest of the band played. Now that was Freddie Kepler's job. That was a man, they'd been used to Freddie Kepler's band. So from the strength of that job, we got three more jobs. Two or three more jobs that we practically made good on. And then about, well it took me about, somewhere else along about six weeks, and I practically got in the band and played. I put the horn, but whatever I couldn't play along, that's how I ruined my lift. You can't see it now because I've been Oliver. But I started in the center of my mouth.
Yeah.

And, pooling with Joe Oliver, it went to the side. Because the first big job that I played, I played the police ball downtown. And all those policemen knew me, they knew Joe Oliver. They'd kid Joe Oliver on one stand and they'd kid me on the other. And, I had a couple of crips. I knew about, when I played that police ball, I knew about five numbers that I could play. Paddymore was one, and Harmony Rag was two, and one was a soldier song we played. I can't think of it now. But, we had crips that we played. And, no matter what the band played, I couldn't play, I'd let the band play. And then, when I could play. What did you call that, the crips?
We called them crips, yeah.

What do you mean? I never heard that term. That's numbers that we knew by head. All numbers, musicians used to play in those days. All bands had a crips. And no matter where he went to play, he'd never play that crips until they jammed him. Just like, we'll say Panama. Well that was our crips. See? That number won me five hundred dollars between me and Joe Oliver.
Well you won the contest then.

Oh yeah. Yeah, because Mr. Groeschel, he was determined because I'm working at one corner, and he's at Pete Lawless at the next corner. See? And Joe, they'd all pass and kick one another at night. If he'd see my boss out there, he'd tell him, say, you better get a band in there, I'd say, cut that fella out there. He can't see, he can't play, he can't blow, nothing. You know, talk about him, kick one another. Yeah, yeah. Now he's got one eye himself, he cock-eyed himself, see? But yet and still, he was just a fella that liked to play the dozens, you know, talk about you.
That's not heard there. He used to kid everybody a lot.

Yeah. Kid everybody, put everybody he met in the dozens. Mm-hmm. Well, we went on with those numbers, like crip numbers that I played, until the band got so good, until Roy got to the place where he spent a little time with me. He'd come down in the evening and show me how to play different numbers and bring two or three numbers longer.
Did you learn to read those then all right? You learned to read music then?

Not then, right away. You didn't learn to learn? No, I'm trying to learn, see? No. But it seemed like I couldn't make it under Roy. And at the time, everything was crowding me, and seemed like I was getting famous and couldn't play. See, I can't play nothing. But at the same time, I kept along with that band. I had most of my band, there was nobody hardly in the band that read anything, but Roy. Roy was the musician from the beginning. But as he'd sit in the band and play, he'd never criticize us, because he didn't want to read no music or do nothing. I don't know where he learned his music at, or how he knew so much, but he'd come right around the band and he'd sit down and he wouldn't try to teach us how to play too much. He'd take his trombone and every time somebody did something and he thought it was good, he'd say that's wonderful, that's great, that's right. And that's how we got by. Well Roy got the most of the jobs. And time by time, after I played about, oh I guess, I don't know how much, about six dances I guess I played, I'll tell you what got the most of the white people. The most of the white people in New Orleans, they had never seen Negroes dress up in white. So I went to work and from my job I bought all the boys white duck pants, band caps, brass band coats, white duck pants.
What color were the coats? Blue, you know like brass band they get, blue.

Blue, you know like a little bit, and white shoes. Well the shoes didn't cost but 75 cents a dollar in those days, see. That white, you can be shoes, see. And the first job that we went on was in Audubon Park. And when we went up there, they had a servant to come to the door and tell us, oh my God, go to the back, don't come in the front, go around the back. And they had us to come in the back. She said, oh you like the crap and everything. The madam said she don't like so and so. Black color people come to the front door, you know better than that. And we explained to her that we didn't know. And to help the job to get worse, we got one man that went up there and we didn't think nothing of it. He didn't have a coat on, he had the white pants. But then she got her husband's coat and put on him after. Now they give us credit for that job. I don't know how we got away with it, nothing like that, but we just come as to playing music. Just that so, until the band, to my idea, didn't keep up with me. Well, why? Because I come right back and went to Mr. Perkins. He charged me a fifth essential lesson. I went over to his house and he taught me the routine of music. And I come and started learning how to go down and see Mr. Eckert at the Grunwald Music Store. I thought it was the greatest thing in the world, go down and buy an orchestration. Fifteen cents. Fifteen cents. Fifteen cents. Fifteen cents. And I'd buy an orchestration and get Mr. Eckert to tell me. He was a salesman in the cloaking place. And I'd come back and Mr. Perkins got so that after I stayed with him a little while, that didn't do me no good. I quit him. So, luck would come on. I don't know how it was, but I got to bumming in the district one night and got in contact with Zoo. And Zoo told me he wanted me to come over to the casino. Is that Zoo Robertson? Zoo Robertson. He lived up in my neighborhood, see, but I had never paid much attention to him. Then, as I did after he found out that I could play, he said he heard that I'd been playing music. So, I followed him the next night that I went down and went over to the casinos. And they had a trumpet player in the band that had been in the band, I think, somewhere along about two years with Armand J. Perkins. His name was Arnold Matoya. Oh, I've heard of him. He was part Spanish. I don't know what Arnold was. He spoke about ten different languages. You know that. Yeah. And he played with Ringling Brothers band. Big band.
He looks a little bit like, his pictures look like Peter Boccage almost.
Huh?
Some pictures I've seen of him, he looks a little bit like Peter Boccage.

Yeah, well, you wouldn't know whether he was a white or what he was, see. But, at those, just around that time he was turning, he was turning to that wine, that drinking, see. One of the greatest trumpet players that ever was. He played with number one Ringling Brothers band, the white band. He sat in the band. And when Zoo carried me there, he always says, a trumpet player? So and so was the case, and he passed me on the show, he said, come on, sit down, here's my horn. That just gave him a chance to go walk around and get his bucket together, see. All musicians that didn't hold up had a bucket, you know. And they drank a claret wine, take a dime. Well, that's where Alno was going down at, just during that time, see. But at the same time, he was one of the greatest I've ever seen, because he could take his horn and hang it up by the vowels. And hang that horn straight, test it for time after time. And he could put his lips up to that horn and let you take a piece of thread and pass through that horn and you'd never hear the blemish of that tone. So I played down there one night in his place practically all night. So after then, it looked like it got set on me. Mr. Groschel told Pierones that it would be better to put me in the band because half the time they couldn't ever see Alno, they didn't know where he was at, see. And he had a wife and I think four children, four of them. So dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Okay, it's going again.

And he went along in the district for a little while after. He didn't play many more places. He just played around. He'd come into places. He never lost friendships with me. And I did come to my head that I wanted to take lessons from him. So I went down to his house and taken lessons. And I found out that I got more out of Anormatwire than I did out of the rest of the people that had showed me anything in the music business. So I rapped so fast and playing in the cabaret at night, and all those white shows come in there. We used them shows in there, all the acts and singing from the Crescent Theatre and all them places used to come.
Was it a regular cabaret or what was it like?
Yeah, it was a cabaret. But we, at those times they used flow shows and choruses. Yeah, what corner was that on? That was on the downtown, back of town by the corner. Downtown. Downtown side.
On Iberville or Custon House?
Custon House, on Custon House.
And what other street? Moray or?
It was, you know where John Lawler was. John Lawler was. Franklin.
Franklin.
Well that was two blocks from the station. Yeah. You know where the new station was there, Bill. Of course they tell me that's not there now.
No, it's all turned out there.

No, the boy was telling me the other day, everything is up by Lee Circle. Union Station. Union Station. All trains come in there. Yeah. Well this was the, when you come off Canal Street and walk one block downtown, then you could look towards the lake and see his sign.
Back two blocks from that time.
Yeah, from that sign, see. Well that's where that was.
Was that the cabaret for white or colored? All white. It was all white. Strictly white. What was the name again, Grossell?
Grossell's Casino.
Eddie Grossell's Casino. Eddie Grossell's Casino. Eddie Grossell's Casino.

Eddie Grossell's Casino. Yeah. You can put that down if you want. And he had, his partner was Del Peter, and his manager was a German Jew, Mr. Hunts. Hunts was his name. And everything was run through transportation of the theaters and all the Spokin people that came in town to shows. Like every show would come to the Crescent Theater or Tulane, don't care if it was, those two theaters sat right together, the Crescent and Tulane, the Opera House, and don't care what sort of show it was, they'd go get those people at night and bring them there and have parties for them. And all the acts that we used in the place was white. Well we got so in a little while after I was there that we played practically all the white acts. Don't care what sort of music they brought in there. If I thought I couldn't play it, if there was a man who thought he couldn't play it, we had an eight piece band. If I thought we couldn't play it, we'd lay down low, or play low where we couldn't. Yeah. Get by with it. In that band, it seemed like that Baby Dutch, Roy Palmer, and all those, that's where the little bad feelings come in there. Because I left that band and went into an organized band. Well the boys wanted me to help them, well I couldn't take Baby Dutch and that because this, Armand J.P. Rons had a band before I went there, see. And naturally they put me in the band and commenced to giving me charge right away and teaching me and everything about the band. That band, that was my second band, that band consists of eight pieces. There was Armand J.P. Rons on violin, George P. Emerson on piano, Archie Walls on bass, Wade Whaley on clarinet.
I knew him, California.
Willie Hightower on trumpet, Elvin Zoo Roberson on trombone. Way left that band went to Oak, Oakland, California.
He played with Ory and Mud Carey and some of that. Yeah, that's right.

He played with Ory and Mud Carey there. But he didn't depend on music too much because he was a decorator. He decorated. But he was a very independent little fellow. He bought a home there, see, in the Uptown, up by Protection Levy. And that band, I stayed with that band two years and seven months. Armand J.P. Rons band, until P. Rons got a job at the St. Charles Hotel. And he took four pieces, or five pieces over there, and turned this band over to me. But he didn't take no man out of this band. He used all string over there in the St. Charles Hotel. I forget now, was it the Gold Room or something? Gold Room, I think it was, and he played in. Well, I kept that band for two years and seven months. And what upset the thing was, somebody come into New York, a performer, scouting around, and they heard of me, and they wanted to hear me play. And that man was, his name was Alexander Tolliver. He was with the Smart Setson. Mr. Parks, what was Parks' name?
What was the name?

Can't think of old man's Parks' initials. But anyhow, it was afterwards, C.W. Parks. C.W. Parks. Then, we got together and I signed a contract to take a band on this show. With the backing of Annole Matoia. See, as I told you, I'd been taken from him. And I agreed to take the show out, if Annole would go on the show, because I couldn't handle it. Because the show was to have a hundred people on it.
Yeah, a good show.

And he promised me, up until the last minute we started rehearsing. Now we rehearsed in the Laperunas, Reno. That was downtown. That was where Harry Wells and all of them put that down there. He was a prize fighter. That was a great big place. The show with it in there. And the first day, I went to Annole's house to get him to come, he wouldn't show up. So, after I done signed the contract, they wouldn't stand for me to back down. They told me, if I had never played on a show, that they would show me everything and help me out and everything. So, I just stayed and scuffled along with it. And as I went along, in the rehearsal, they set off and helped me out with musicians. The first musicians, they got in my band. Now I got Elvin Sue Robison from New Orleans. Eddie Robison, call him Rabbit on drums. Oh, yeah. You heard of him?
I've heard of him.

Eddie Robison. Oh, he was a good one. He's the one that Robeshoe's drummer taught how to play drums. Walter Bundy. That was Robeshoe's drummer. Then he taught Eddie Robison how to play drums. Zoo, Eddie Robison, myself, John Porter, you heard of him, he's in the Orleans, Bond in the Orleans, bass, and Dave, Dave Jones wasn't the microphone. That's right. One of the sweetest melaphone players you've ever wanted yet. Well, I brought away a brass band. And all the men that I couldn't get to fill the band, like Reed men, I got plenty of Reed men in the Orleans, like Béchet and all them, but I got to the place then where I carried my music with me. Well, I kind of put on airs a little bit with the fellas at the time, you know, and played. Well, we set off, the first man we got was Fred Culey, clarinet player. He had only been in the United States of America eight years when I hired him. He come from somewhere in South America and had never played around. He couldn't understand nothing he said. Yeah. And after we got him, then we was lucky about two weeks after to get King Phillips. He was a clarinet player. You heard of him? No, I don't think so. He was from North Carolina or somewhere. I don't think so. Fred, King Phillips. Well, there were two of them. It was just as great as you ever want to hear. I kept on until I formed that band to 18 pieces. And then we hit the road. And I stayed on the road from end of 1915 until, what year did we come here? Of course, we were talking about that tonight, how old my oldest boy was. But I don't think it was 21 when we come out. William wasn't born in 21.
You were born in 22.
No. Well, we let it that way. We come in Chicago about that time.
About 1921 or 22.
Yeah, we came here in Chicago.
When your oldest boy was born.

Yeah, when my oldest boy was born, see. Then, I done had just about as much soaking as I wanted in that line of business. When I came here in Chicago, I had offers from Charlie Cook. He had a band, Patty Harmon's Dreamland Hems, Westside. I had an offer from Dave Payton, had the band in the Grand Theater. I had offers from two, three bands. What was the drummer's name that had the band at the-
The band's two?
Bertrand or Jim- Schillers. No, at the Entertainers. Oh. The one that died. Can't think of his-
Wichler.
Huh?
Wichler?
Yeah, that's it. Yeah, I had all- What was the name again?
The drummer?
Yeah.
What was his name? John Wicklett. Oh, Wicklett.
Oh, yes. John Wicklett.
John Wicklett. Sure, I've heard of him, yes. Yeah, well, he was the great-

He was the drummer. I didn't know he played drums. He was the first man that had a set of gold drums. People used to go over there at night just to see those gold and pearl drums that he had. See, and he built the reputation. Well, I played in Chicago around and-
There's one thing, excuse me for interrupting again, but since you're talking about your wife coming up here with you and all, when were you married and-
Well, I was with Toliver Smutsets when I met her. She had the band on the number one show, and this show that I was with was number two.
Where did the wife come from?
Charleston, South Carolina.
Charleston, South Carolina.

She was born in Charleston, South Carolina. And she's been playing piano since she was, what was she, 12 years old? Yeah. She took lessons from a teacher in Charleston, South Carolina, when she started to get 12. And kept that up until, I don't know when your mother, your father decided to send you to Boston. But she went to Boston Conservatory, and she's got a sheepskin of-
I knew that, I'd always heard that Mrs. Hightower is a wonderful pianist.

Oh, yes. And she played at the Dixieland Theater in Charleston, South Carolina. See, her father was a railroad man. I don't think he played any music, but he sang. And she kept up that music and got professional. And it was a great thing for me to, for people to tell me on the show about her band, and for her to write to them and tell her about our band on the show. Well, it got to the place where her friend, one of her friends, got my picture and sent to her. I'd never seen her picture. And then she wanted to meet me and meet her, so finally we, the two shows met in Charleston, South Carolina. And that's where I had a chance to meet her. And it was just like you see it, for 40-some odd years, from the first day I met her, she's never been away from me.
That's wonderful. Yes. Able to work together then. Yeah.

Well, that's what they claims hurt me in the music business. They said that I would have been better off if I'd have never married my wife. But, I don't know, it was just one of these things that when I started out in the music business, I couldn't see a woman piano player. And I swore to everybody that a woman couldn't play music like a man. A lot of people used to think that, yeah.
Yeah, that's what you mean.

Didn't want no woman have nothing to do with no music. And I practically sold up. They left my honing home until we come over to rehearsal. And when I come over to rehearsal, she came in. And I opened the briefcase and handed her the opening chorus. And the opening chorus was named Boy and Girl.
Excuse me.
Yeah. Sure. And when I come to find out, she's the one who made the manuscript.
Oh, really? That's so pretty good.

And I asked her, could she play it? And when she sat down to the piano and I put the music up on the piano foot and I say, hit the introduction of that. She hit the introduction and turned the head off.
Played a jump. See?

Yeah. And a boyfriend of mine that knew her before he knew me, he's the one who bought the ring, you see, on her hand and the marriage license. And we got married. And we got married. In two, three months afterwards. After you met her. After I met her. Three months afterwards. And we've been going ever since. Now when we got here in Chicago, I had decided to stay here in Chicago about nine weeks. And then I thought I would go to New York and stay about nine weeks because her father wanted me to open business. I wanted to go in business. I had taken up arranging and I wanted to arrange. I thought I could arrange. And I was going back to Charleston, South Carolina and opening up business. But after I got here, after all the offers that I got, Baby Hall, he's another drummer probably.
Yes, I knew him. I knew him. He played just not in our country.
He had a brother by the name of Minor Hall.
I know him too.
He was in Los Angeles.
Kid Ory.
Kid Ory. He was with Kid Ory in there.
Yeah, I knew both of them.

Yeah. Well, Baby was working with me at the entertainers. Well, he got me the job over there, see, with Carol Dixon. Well, I didn't care for it very much so I just quit that altogether and I wanted to build my band myself. So I just went to work and bought a car and went out on the north side and went around places and advertised the band. Finally, we got out of my work, we got six years and a half work of the band on the Gold Coast and over Chicago with the band under her name. The band never was under my name. After I found it in her night, Eudora Nighthawks. Eudora came from a dancing class, was at Fortis and State. That was Mason Hall. And the man that used to run dancing classes here in Chicago. Every night in the week there was a dancing class somewhere. Well, he had shows, he put on shows and he would get jobs like at Congress Hotel, Eudora Beach Hotel and all them places. He'd take 45 and 50 people. He was like Joneses with the choir around here, you know, take a big bunch of, yeah. And then he built a band right along with it. And they helped both him and what we did, we named the band Lolly Hightower and Eudora Nighthawks band. Coincidence that happened, after we had that name going, Joe Saunders and Dale Coon come in here with the Nighthawks. Oh sure, yeah. They come to St. Louis. And he says that he had had the name for a long time. Well, we didn't squabble over it at all. We met out here at 35th and State Street one night and went in a restaurant and sat down and talked. Well, Joe Saunders was kind of a hard fellow to talk with, but Dale Coon was all right. Dale Coon was the drummer, see. Well, he was a pretty good fellow. Joe Saunders was the piano player.
Yeah, we could hear him already.

Yeah, we got all the greatest bands you want to hear. That was a really a good band. They were really great. And we got along pretty good, but most of those fellows, as we will get back to myself about recording and numbers recording, I'm something like Freddie Kepler was if you never heard about it. I heard he wouldn't play or nothing. Anybody around going to catch anything? He laid it on down and he said, go on about your business, you ain't going to steal nothing from me. See? Well, that's the way I was. And then where else we'd go at night and somebody would say so-and-so, and they'd ask her, they asked my wife, tell your husband to play so-and-so. I said, no, there'll be no playing. I laid it on down. See? Until they gone. And when they gone, then I'd play. Well, that's the way Freddie Kepler was. I doubt whether Freddie Kepler made over one number, and that number was, can't think of it right now, but he wrote, he published, he let him publish that number with Charlie Cook's band in Patty Harmon's Dreamer. It's one number. The other side, they had to put another number on there. He just had one number. Oh, yeah.
There was one that's called Messin' Around.
Scissors Grinder.
Huh?
Scissors Grinder. What's that?
Scissors Grinder. Yeah. Sure, yeah, I have that number. What is that? The Scissors Grinder. You know, the scissors. Scissors! That was the number. That was the number. That was the number.

That was the number. And he got a little more ingenious because they told him he'd have to get out of it. But he died before he ever played anymore. And it wouldn't change his style for nothing. Well, I knew back in all the times that I was coming along that the time was changing. Well, up until 1918 they hadn't got a change yet. See, because still the white musicians were still criticizing the Negro musicians were playing music because they said that it never would last nowhere. That putting, they say, a beer bucket over a trumpet or something like that will never work. And every time they'd see me and I'd reach down and come in the place and I'd take my beer bucket or something and put it over there and come and say, womp, womp, womp, like that and make the horn talk like me and Freddie used to play because that's what we feel like doing, like whatever your name was. If we knew you, I could call your name on that mouthpiece just the same as I could out without saying anything. See? We talked on the horns. That's what I heard. That's right. Yeah. We played chicken reel and numbers like that. that boy, we played like the number goes, and you'd hear me say, and Bambi said, and I'd say, and then I'd say, and all those kind of things. So those were things that we had an idea that they had to catch off us to beat us playing. But as I come along, I told most of the boys, regardless of what you know, the freak that you can play on an instrument, learn how to read music. That's the greatest thing. And I'm so glad that I did since even I met my wife and the teachers that I went with, too, taught me how to read. And it helped me so that men like down in Chicago theater, those men down like that, when I went off, I didn't know how much my music went, met to me until I left here and went on the off-hand circuit and met them different white bands playing on the stand. We left here with fourteen pieces. And without a word of doubt, I wouldn't tell you a story, everywhere we'd go, and we'd open them first shows, and that white band would sit down on that pit at night and look at us like this. And when the show was off, they'd say, I want to meet your first trumpet player. And that's how I got my courage. It all come down. I met my greatest band, two of the greatest bands. One was in, uh, Pass, where's Dominic? Where did Dominic? Where did I tell you Dominic, the boy, cut Dominic's wrist about the girl?
In California.

We had to leave Dominic there. We left Dominic there until we got to Long Beach. They kept him in the hospital two weeks. I can't think of that band leader's name, one of the greatest men there was. Then I had the pleasure of shaking hands with the man that made C.G. Conn's first Wonderhorn. That was, uh, the man had the band in Long Beach.
Can you ask me then?
Yeah, I can't think of his name now. But he was the man that made the Wonderhorn.
What kind of a horn do you like best? Well, C.G.
Conn. Conn most of the time. Yeah. C.G. Conn's first time. I had the horn stolen from me here. Oh, wow.
So I'm using El, uh, Selma now.
Selma. Yeah.
Did you always use the cornet or did you change the trumpet?
Oh, I changed the trumpet.
When did you change about?

I changed, I changed when I got here, didn't I? I was using the Wonder, wasn't I? Yeah. The Wonder was, Herbert L. Clark was his name. Oh, yeah, sure. It's in the Suzy's band. Yeah, he had the band, yeah. He made a horn that the tuning slide was in the back called a Wonder. You could hold it. And if it didn't suit your ears, all you had to do is touch it. Well, that was a cornet. Now, I changed to a Holton during the time I got a Holton, a brass Holton. I didn't keep that very long. But I bought two CG corn, cornets. I've never had a CG corn trumpet until I had this Selma. And after this horn was stolen from me, I had a chance to lock up on this horn cheap. And I bought it at a pawn shop down here on State in Van Buren. And just before you go, I'll show it to you. It keeps it locked up. Oh, yeah. Yeah, it keeps it locked up so you can. I don't leave it out. I'm just so afraid to keep it in the house almost, see. So, I haven't had my hands on it. But after we got here and played on and looked like I made, I guess it's like one of those things you make too much money and haven't got the schooling or the knowledge to do what you would like to do with those things. And nobody to help you and you start out with just money and no brains. I bought a flat building. And after I bought that building, I turned around and bought another building. Two flat buildings, 4914 Forestville and 450 East 50th Street. Then I bought 37 watts at 115th in May. That was just lots. Well, we lost all of that.
I hope you didn't lose it all in the depression.
We lost every, in 18 months, we didn't have a dime.
So many people did that all over the country.

We didn't have a dime. After 18 months, I didn't have a dime. Everything closed down after 1928. And musicians around here just like, whatever you say Preston Jackson, I always think about him. Because the boy was just in his primes, they're coming up, see. And he's got a wife, I don't know how many children he's got now. I don't know who they are. He had three or four of them. And the boy was just coming along, see, and it just upset everybody so you couldn't get nothing. There was musicians around just doing anything, see. Well that's what persuaded the most of the music in 28. Because when things did open up back in 32 and 33, they didn't open back up in the music world. No. They opened in something else. It just worked like we did. Now May's Sugar Place out here, they had a lot of boys in there from Yarns too. They had May's in there. You never heard of him, did you? No. He was a violin player.
May's Sugar Factory out here in Commercial Avenue? No, I didn't know about it.

Well there was, he was born and raised in Yarns, May's was. And he, after he got out there, he formed the union and he got the boys from Local 208 out there, see. And he formed a band out there. Well I used to play out there with them. I was going to work out there with them. But in later years, he made so much money, he built a home right out there, see. And he gave up the working, see, and he's sitting down now. But at the same time, why? I don't know, it just, afterwards it's just one of those things. I'm here now. I moved in here with pretty good spirit that I would make good.
Soon as I moved in here, she got sick.

And I had started me a house. Last, just before it got cold, I got the roof and everything on. I've got everything on the exterior finished. Just got to finish the end till. She's warning me now, but I go there. I tell her I can't move out there because I need just about a thousand dollars to get finished the place.
You have to finish it up before you move in and now.
But the house is built, everything is paper, don't want a dime. See, I'm building a Connell style house, two story house, five rooms.
And how far, where is it now?

That's at 9239 South Parnell Avenue. 9339 South Parnell Avenue. Don't know the number one house. No, no, no. But at the same time... I've got that going pretty good. That's... Oh, yeah, that's nice. Two stories. Yeah. That's... Oh, yeah, that's a nice house. That's the way it looks. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Everything paper. Yeah.
All I want now is just, I'm trying to get my heat in there and the wire. And I get the wire and the heat in there, I can move out of this place. I get comfortable.

It just worries me and others to death. See. But I'm doing the best I can for my age. That's better not trying to work too hard. That's the only trouble. I've been rucked. See. And I'm... and he and I can move out of this place. I get comfortable, it just worries me the other day. But I'm doing the best I can for my age. You better not try to work too hard.
No, that's the only trouble. I've been roughed, see.

And I'm six to eight years old. So you know, I got to kind of take it easy, see. That's the only trouble. And my work keeps me going, see. I get up in the morning about quarter to four. And I leave here just about 4.30. And I don't get back in the house until 4.30 or 5 o'clock in the evening. When I work in eight hours. Now if I'm working ten hours or twelve hours, I don't get back in the house until seven or eight o'clock at night.

I'm going to try to finish this up so that we can get some rest. Yeah. I wanted to ask a little bit about the records you made. There's hardly room on here. We can start it here and I'll run it in another five minutes and we'll be through. Yeah. Did you make some records with Richard M. Jones too? Yeah. Do you remember which company or what the titles were and who else was in the band?
No, I remember the band because I used all of my band. Just Richard on piano.
Yeah.

And he used me and he used my clarinet player as Fred Palm and he used John Lindsay, my trombone player. Oh yeah. He's in y'all. He's in old now jazz. He played bass too. That's what you knew him is because in New Orleans he played bass when he's... Yeah. Thank you.

segments.title: Birth in Nashville, move to New Orleans, work at the ice cream company
segments.summary: Hightower gives his birth (Nashville, 1889), the move to New Orleans at six, and driving a wagon for the ice cream company until he quit in 1915 to play music.

segments.title: Boyhood across the street from Joe Oliver
segments.summary: He recalls playing in the street with Joe Oliver as boys, living across from each other and attending different schools.

segments.title: First instruments: cornet, then a one-string soapbox bass and serenading
segments.summary: He tried cornet, then made a one-string bass from a soapbox and played with friends serenading neighbours at night, dodging a policeman.

segments.title: Opening an ice cream parlor and buying a saloon at Sixth and Rampart
segments.summary: At 17 he opened an ice cream parlor on Rampart Street, hired Myknee Jones on piano, and bought a saloon he was too young to enter.

segments.title: Running the Sixth and Rampart lawn ground and hiring Freddie Keppard's band
segments.summary: With Bab Frank he opened an open-air lawn ground, built a bandstand and hired Freddie Keppard's band, discussing the guitarist, perhaps Brock Mumford.

segments.title: Roy Palmer brings him a brass horn
segments.summary: After two summers Roy Palmer brought him a horn, which he polished with brass polish and started fooling with.

segments.title: His parents' music: father's cornet, mother's harp, church
segments.summary: His father was a barber and brass-band cornetist in Nashville, his mother played harp, piano and guitar; he recalls little church music.

segments.title: Learning from Roy Palmer and the visit from teacher Dave Perkins
segments.summary: Roy shows him how to blow the horn and proposes a band; trombonist Dave Perkins hears him practising and warns him to learn music.

segments.title: First band job: Pep Wallace, Baby Dodds, and clowning with the horn
segments.summary: He forms his first band with Roy Palmer, Baby Dodds on a makeshift drum kit, and plays his first concert and dance mostly clowning.

segments.title: The police ball and the 'cribs' repertoire
segments.summary: At the police ball he knew about five numbers, his 'cribs', tunes a band always had in reserve, and one won him $500 against Joe Oliver.

segments.title: Joe Oliver and the rivalry of the dozens
segments.summary: Oliver worked the next corner, and the two traded insults and played the dozens.

segments.title: Roy Palmer as unspoken teacher; reading music; white uniforms
segments.summary: Roy helped by encouraging rather than teaching; Hightower struggles to read, then buys the band white ducks and blue coats that impress white New Orleans.

segments.title: First job at Audubon Park, lessons with Perkins, and joining Zue Robertson at the casino
segments.summary: They are sent to the back door at Audubon Park; he takes lessons from Perkins, buys orchestrations, and Zue Robertson takes him to the casino to sit in for Arnold Metoyer.

segments.title: Arnold Metoyer, the great trumpeter who was drinking
segments.summary: Metoyer, who played with Ringling Brothers, had astonishing tone and control but was going downhill, so management put Hightower in his chair.

segments.title: Lessons from Metoyer and playing for the cabaret shows
segments.summary: After tape change, Hightower says he learned most from Metoyer and describes playing the cabaret for visiting theatre acts.

segments.title: Where Eddie Grunewald's Casino stood
segments.summary: Russell and Hightower work out the location of the all-white cabaret near Canal Street and Customhouse, and confirm the name Grunewald's Casino.

segments.title: Playing for the cabaret acts and joining Armand Piron's eight-piece band
segments.summary: The casino's backers, white acts and the hurt feelings with Roy Palmer and Baby Dodds; he lists Piron's band lineup and later takes it over.

segments.chapter: On the road with the show
segments.title: Alexander Tolliver's offer and forming a show band
segments.summary: Tolliver's show scouts him; after rehearsals, with Metoyer failing to show, he builds a band with Zue Robertson, Eddie Robinson and others and grows it to 18 pieces.

segments.title: Arriving in Chicago and the offers there
segments.summary: After touring from 1915, they reach Chicago about 1921-22 and he gets offers from Charlie Cook, Dave Payton and others, with talk of drummer John Wicklett.

segments.title: Meeting his wife, a pianist from Charleston
segments.summary: He met her while the two shows were on tour; she is a Boston Conservatory-trained pianist from Charleston, and they finally met there.

segments.title: His doubts about a woman pianist and her first rehearsal
segments.summary: He swore a woman could not play like a man until she played the opening chorus from her own manuscript at rehearsal.

segments.title: Marriage and plans on arriving in Chicago; the Hall brothers
segments.summary: They married three months after meeting; he planned to stay briefly in Chicago, before offers and mentions of Baby and Minor Hall.

segments.title: Leading Lottie Hightower and Her Nighthawks in Chicago
segments.summary: After quitting Carroll Dickerson's band he built his own, worked six and a half years on the Gold Coast, and sorted out the Nighthawks name with Joe Sanders and Coon.

segments.title: Freddie Keppard's refusal to record and the Scissor Grinder
segments.summary: Hightower compares his own guarded playing to Keppard, who recorded only one number, 'Scissor Grinder', fearing others would steal his ideas.

segments.title: Changing times, talking horns, reading music, and touring white bands
segments.summary: He remembers white criticism of mutes, how horns 'talked', his advice to learn to read, and how white pit bands respected his section on tour.

segments.title: Touring to Long Beach and the Conn Wonderhorn
segments.summary: A band member was left in hospital in California; he met the Wonderhorn maker and says he prefers Conn horns.

segments.title: Switching to trumpet and buying Chicago buildings
segments.summary: He changed horns, bought a Selmer secondhand, and recalls spending his earnings on flat buildings and lots that were later lost.

segments.title: The Depression ends the music business
segments.summary: He lost everything in 18 months after 1928; music work vanished and he mentions Preston Jackson and a violinist who ran a sugar-place band.

segments.title: Present life: building a house and working long days
segments.summary: His wife became ill, he is building a two-story house, and he describes his early-morning day job at his age.

segments.title: Records made with Richard M. Jones
segments.summary: Russell asks about recordings with Richard M. Jones; Hightower recalls using his own band, with Jones on piano.
